title: Real-Time Intravital Multiphoton Microscopy to Visualize Focused Ultrasound and Microbubble Treatments to Increase Blood-Brain Barrier Permeability
protocol: Prepare the materials needed for cranial window surgery and ultrasound-microbubble treatments.
Sterilize tools and materials.
Ensure availability of a sterile surgical space.
Prepare pre- and post-surgery drug administration materials for chronic cranial windows.
Check the physical integrity of the transducer for cracks and dents.
Inspect electrodes on the top and side of the transducer to ensure they are intact.
Deposit cyanoacrylate glue into a small dish.
Spread a thin layer of glue onto the surface of the transducer using an applicator.
Place the transducer onto the glass coverslip.
Press down firmly for 20-30 seconds.
Check for bubbles between the transducer and the coverslip.
If bubbles are present, remove the coverslip and repeat from depositing cyanoacrylate glue.
Cure the assembly overnight at room temperature.
Replace the coverslip if it is cracked or has debris from the previous experiment.
Submerge the transducer and coverslip in acetone for 20 min to dissolve the glue.
Gently pull on the coverslip with forceps to check if the glue has dissolved.
Check once every 10 min to avoid prolonged acetone exposure.
Choose carrier gases based on project aims and veterinarian advice.
Perform a toe pinch to check the animal's plane of anesthesia.
Weigh the animal to determine dosage of dextran, microbubbles, and drugs.
Remove fur from the animal's head.
Place the animal onto a stereotactic frame.
Insert a 27 g catheter into a tail vein for systemic circulation access.
Transfer the animal onto the stereotactic frame and switch anesthesia to nose cone.
Maintain the animal's core temperature at 37 °C using a heat source.
Monitor animal temperature with a rectal probe.
Monitor animal physiology using a pulse oximeter.
Apply ophthalmic ointment.
Inject appropriate pre-surgery analgesic and/or anti-inflammatory drugs (see Table of Materials).
Check the plane of anesthesia prior to surgery.
Check the animal's heart rate, O2 saturation, respiratory rate, and temperature before starting cranial window surgery.
Remove fur on the head using a depilatory cream and/or fur clippers.
Remove fur from between the eyes to the anterior half of the neck.
Wash the scalp with alternating wipes of betadine and 70% EtOH for chronic surgeries after fur removal.
Prepare the surgical space for sterile surgery.
Maintain sterility until Step 2.15.
Lift skin between the eyes using forceps to expose the parietal bones.
Remove the skin to expose the parietal bones with curved scissors.
Apply firm pressure with a cotton swab if there is bleeding from the skull or scalp.
Stop bleeding before proceeding to the next step.
Push back and adhere skin to the skull using liquid cyanoacrylate glue or tissue adhesive for acute surgeries.
Remove the periosteum covering the outer surface of the skull using cotton swabs.
Using an operating microscope, outline a circle on the parietal bone to mark the desired location for the cranial window.
Avoid marking over the sagittal suture, lambda, and bregma areas.
Use a dental drill with a 0.5 mm drill burr at medium speed to outline the cranial window.
Draw an outline of the cranial window onto the skull using a marker and stencil if needed.
For rats, use a rectangular shape for easier drilling and switch between a 0.7 mm bit to outline and a 0.5 mm bit to complete the drilling.
Apply gentle pressure with the drill bit while drilling.
Drip saline onto the skull during drilling to prevent overheating.
Alternate between drilling and cooling until the bone island separates from the rest of the skull.
Check the drilling progress by applying gentle pressure on the bone island using forceps or the drill bit.
Use fine forceps to grasp the edges or upper compact bone layer of the bone island for removal.
Keep brain moist by applying a pre-soaked surgical sponge.
Place surgical sponge on bleeding region if bleeding is observed.
Do not proceed until bleeding has ceased.
Remove dura with fine forceps under high magnification if necessary and thick.
Pick up glass coverslip with forceps for cranial window placement.
Place drop of saline onto one side of the coverslip.
Maneuver coverslip over hole in skull to place cranial window.
Ensure no air bubbles are present under the coverslip.
Prepare the 1% (w/v) agarose solution.
Add 0.1 g of agarose and 10 mL of PBS or saline into a beaker.
Boil the solution until the agarose has fully dissolved.
Withdraw ~ 0.5 mL of agarose into a 1 mL syringe.
Ensure the temperature of the agarose approximates body temperature before use.
Deposit agarose liberally onto the coverslip of the cranial window.
Apply firm pressure such that there is minimal agarose between the transducer and the cranial window.
Cut away excess agarose from the circumference of the transducer's coverslip using a spatula or scalpel.
Spread a layer of cyanoacrylate glue over the circumference of the transducer's coverslip, extending to the skull.
Position the animal under the objective lens.
Ensure the objective lens is centered in the ring transducer.
Ensure the objective lens is parallel with the transducer.
Fill the center of the ring transducer with deionized and degassed water if using a water-immersion objective lens.
Start with the objective lens in its highest position.
Slowly lower the objective lens until it is within the ring transducer.
Check the Z-position of the objective lens through the eyepiece to ensure it is in-plane with the surface of the brain.
Ensure the objective lens does not collide with the transducer or coverslip by eye.
Prepare the multiphoton microscope for imaging.
Add PBS to the vial of dextran as per manufacturer's instructions.
Vortex the dextran solution for 1-3 min to ensure full dissolution.
Inject the dextran solution into the tail vein.
Ensure that the objective lens is parallel to the brain using eyepieces.
Tilt the animal to correct for XZ and YZ misalignments.
Select a field-of-view in a multiphoton microscope.
Set up an XYZ scan before ultrasound exposure for baseline image acquisition.
Connect all BNC cables correctly.
Set up an XYZT image scan to capture image stacks before, during, and after ultrasound-microbubble treatments.
Prepare the microbubbles following manufacturer's instructions.
Inject the microbubbles into the tail vein.
Begin imaging immediately after injection.
Ensure consistent injection rate if using an infusion pump.
Enable concurrent microbubble injection and imaging.
Access the tail vein easily without exposing detectors to ambient light.
Begin sonication.
Continue multiphoton imaging throughout the duration of sonication and following the end of sonication.
Export image stacks.
Analyze images with image analysis software such as Olympus Fluoview, ImageJ/FIJI, Bitplane Imaris, or ThermoFisher Scientific Amira.
Use programming tools like Python or MATLAB for image analysis.
